description: Per-translation overlay glossary for Atra-ḫasīs (the project's second Akkadian-source text, after Adapa). v1.0.0 covered Tablet I (anthropogony): the *lullû* primeval-human keyword; the *inūma ilū awīlum* frame-crux (comparative vs identity, with the lens-discipline non-selection of the identity reading recorded); the *eṭemmu* ghost/spirit divine-element (flagged for future central promotion); the Wê-ila / *ṭēmu* double-pun (the anthropogonic heart); the *šīru/damu/ṭiṭṭu* flesh/blood/clay triad (flagged as a CENTRAL-GLOSSARY candidate, cross-corpus to Hebrew *bāśār/dām/ʿāfār–ḥōmer* → Gen 2:7, deferred to the separate central-glossary Python step); and the minor cruxes *uppu* (drum/heartbeat/ghost-token), *urûtam* (freedom/birth-stool), and *ruʾtu* (spittle). v1.1.0 (semver-minor, additions only) extends coverage to Tablet II (the population-control cycle) and Tablet III (the Flood): the *rigmu/ḫubūru* clamor-of-overpopulation flood-cause (flagged as a CENTRAL-GLOSSARY candidate, cross-corpus to Hebrew *ḥāmās*/*ṣeʿāqâ*, deferred to the central step); *Namtar* the plague/fate-god; *Adad*'s inverted drought-role (rain WITHHELD, the inverse of the flood-instrument sense — a scope-note over the central Adad entry); the offering-concentration / shaming-the-god stratagem (with the Tablet-II *ṭēmu* = 'plan/scheme' sense held DISTINCT from the Tablet-I anthropogonic *ṭēmu*-pun — the two are NOT conflated); the population-control affliction-vocabulary (*šuruppû*, *diʾu*, *bubūtu*, *idrānu*); the *Atra-ḫasīs* name-etymology gloss ('exceedingly wise'); the reed-wall (*igāru*/*kikkišu*) oath-loophole; the *napišta bulliṭ* 'keep life alive' flood-instruction; and the etiological population-limit cluster that closes the poem — *pašittu* (the infant-snatching demoness), *lā ālittu* (non-bearing women), the celibate priestess classes *ugbabtu*/*entu*/*igiṣītu* under the *ikkibu* birth-taboo, and settled *mūtu* (mortality). Cross-corpus foundational vocabulary already carried by central entries (*dullu*, *ṭiṭṭu*/clay, DINGIR-prefix-prose-drop, Anunnaki/Igigi, birth-goddess cluster, lacuna-bracket, and the FLOOD cluster: *abūbu*, *eleppu*, gods-like-flies, the flood-council/decree/oath and survivor-name entries) is referenced by id in the chapter glossaryRefs and flagged in the Editor reports for Akkadian-side appliesTo activation in the separate central step; NOT touched here.

entries.partOfSpeech: convention: chapter-title and meta-conventions for the Atra-ḫasīs overlay
entries.literal: (not applicable — meta)
entries.standardEnglish: (not applicable — meta)
entries.wohChoice: chapter-title 'Atra-ḫasīs, Tablet I — When the gods, like man: the labor of the Igigi and the creation of humankind from clay and a slain god's flesh' — short canonical name + descriptive subtitle naming the labor-frame and the creation core; follows the Flood Story / Adapa descriptive long-form title precedent.
entries.rationale: Chapter-title convention for Atra-ḫasīs follows the Mesopotamian-arc precedent (Flood Story, Adapa): the canonical composition-name plus a descriptive subtitle that names the two curated spans — the corvée-labor frame (the Igigi bearing the *dullu* of the senior gods) and the anthropogonic core (humankind fashioned from clay mixed with a slain god's flesh and blood). The subtitle opens with the celebrated title-line *inūma ilū awīlum* to situate the composition in its own incipit-tradition. No new project-wide convention is introduced; the title is descriptive and lens-free — it names what the text narrates, not what the Wheel of Heaven program reads into it.

entries.literal: (not applicable — meta)
entries.standardEnglish: (not applicable — meta)

Per-line sign values may contain reconstruction errors; sense-of-line is well-attested across the cited editions (Lambert–Millard 1969; George & Al-Rawi 1996; Foster 2005) and reflects scholarly consensus.
entries.rationale: Atra-ḫasīs is a MOAT TEXT: no usable public-domain English translation exists, so the Wheel of Heaven program renders its own English from a best-effort Akkadian reconstruction. The source file's `verificationStatus` — *best-effort-reconstruction-pending-verification; sign-by-sign transliteration pending collation against Lambert–Millard 1969 and eBL L.1.1* — is preserved unchanged by the Editor in both the source file and the chapter `translation.verificationStatus` field. The Editor's lens-discipline and glossary work operates on the **sense-of-line** (well-attested across the cited editions), which is independent of the sign-level transliteration verification; the two pipelines converge at the Reviewer pass. This draft curates the labor-frame (I:1–71) and the creation core (I:189–276); intervening spans are flagged with editorial-selection gap notes and are not reconstructed here. A downstream collation-pass against Lambert–Millard 1969 and eBL L.1.1 is requested for sign-level verification.

entries.strongs: CAD L 242–243 s.v. lullû; AHw 561 s.v. lullû ('Urmensch')
entries.partOfSpeech: Akkadian noun — the primeval/first human as a fashioned creature
entries.literal: the primeval one / the first(-fashioned) man
entries.standardEnglish: man (Lambert–Millard 1969); 'a mortal' / 'human' (Foster 2005); 'primitive / savage man' (CAD L 242)
entries.wohChoice: retain *lullû* transliterated, glossed 'primeval human' on first occurrence (I:192)
entries.rationale: CAD L 242 and AHw 561 attest *lullû* as the primeval/first man specifically as a fashioned creature (AHw 'Urmensch'); the term recurs at Enūma Eliš VI:6 (*lullâ lū amēlu* 'let a lullû-man be'), the Babylonian creation-of-man line. Retaining the word untranslated with a neutral gloss avoids over-committing between Lambert–Millard's flat 'man,' CAD's 'primitive/savage man,' and Foster's 'mortal' — none of which is consensus — while preserving the technical anthropogonic keyword for the reader's audit. Cross-corpus to Sumerian *lu2-u18-lu* and thematically to Hebrew *ʾādām*. No lens is carried: 'primeval human' is the neutral philological value the three renderings share, not an engineered-being reading.

entries.strongs: CAD A/2 48–57 s.v. awīlu; Lambert–Millard 1969, 42–43, 146–150; Foster 2005, 227
entries.partOfSpeech: Akkadian nominal clause — the title-line of the poem
entries.literal: When the gods (were / like) man
entries.standardEnglish: When the gods like man (Lambert–Millard 1969, comparative); 'When the gods were man' (Foster 2005, identity title-rendering)
entries.wohChoice: 'When the gods, like man,' — the Lambert–Millard comparative reading retained as the critical-edition baseline; the identity reading documented, not adopted
entries.rationale: The syntax of *awīlum* in the incipit is genuinely disputed: (a) comparative/predicative '(as/like) man' (Lambert–Millard 1969; von Soden) — the gods themselves did man's-work before humankind existed; (b) identity 'the gods were man,' i.e. the gods were then the labor-force (Foster's title-rendering 'When the gods were man'); (c) *awīlum* as the start of the labor-clause. The Editor retains (a), the critical-edition baseline, as the most cautious reading and the one matching the line-numbering authority. **Explicit lens-discipline record:** reading (b) is the more Wheel-of-Heaven-congenial rendering (the gods as a mundane, physically-laboring population), but the accuracy-above-lens rule forbids selecting a reading because it flatters the lens; both are defensible and the sense is close either way (the gods bore the labor before humans). The identity reading is documented in commentary, not imported into the text.

entries.strongs: CAD E 397–401 s.v. eṭemmu; AHw 263 s.v. eṭemmu ('Totengeist')
entries.partOfSpeech: Akkadian noun — the ghost/spirit of the dead; here the divine element persisting in humankind
entries.literal: ghost, spirit of the dead
entries.standardEnglish: ghost (Lambert–Millard 1969); spirit / ghost (Foster 2005)
entries.wohChoice: 'a spirit (eṭemmu)' — retain the technical term with the gloss 'spirit'; 'ghost' noted as the Lambert–Millard baseline
entries.rationale: CAD E 397 and AHw 263 define *eṭemmu* as the ghost/spirit of a dead person — specifically the ancestral ghost sustained by *kispu* funerary offerings, not a generic 'soul.' In Atra-ḫasīs the *eṭemmu* is the enduring DIVINE element left in humankind from the slain god's flesh (I:217, 227): the human being is part-clay, part-divine, and the divine part is precisely the *eṭemmu*. The rendering also anchors the etymological pun *ṭēmu → eṭemmu* (I:222), whereby the slain god's 'intelligence' (*ṭēmu*) becomes the human 'ghost' (*eṭemmu*) — see `we-ila-temu-anthropogonic-pun-atrahasis`. Retaining the transliterated term with the neutral gloss 'spirit' preserves the pun and the technical sense; 'ghost' is the critical-edition baseline. **Flagged as a future central-promotion candidate:** the *eṭemmu* recurs across the Akkadian corpus (Gilgamesh XII, the *kispu* texts, the Descent of Ištar) and is cross-corpus to Hebrew *ruaḥ* / *nefeš* and Eccl 12:7 ('the spirit returns to God who gave it'); promotion is deferred to a future Editor pass, not committed here.

entries.strongs: CAD Ṭ 85–98 s.v. ṭēmu; Lambert–Millard 1969, 56–59, 153; Moran 1970; Abusch 1998
entries.partOfSpeech: Akkadian proper name + noun — the slaughtered god and his 'intelligence'
entries.literal: Wê-ila, who had intelligence / reason
entries.standardEnglish: Wê-ila who had intelligence (Lambert–Millard 1969); the god who had sense / rationality (Foster 2005)
entries.wohChoice: 'Wê-ila, who had ṭēmu (intelligence)' — retain the name and retain *ṭēmu* with gloss; the double pun surfaced in commentary
entries.rationale: This is the etymological heart of Mesopotamian anthropogony. (1) The slain god's NAME: OB *we-e i-la* is read variously Wê-ila / Wê-e / Aw-ila / Ilawēla / (later Geštu-e); the Editor follows Lambert–Millard's Wê-ila, the reading that carries the double pun. (2) *ṭēmu* (CAD Ṭ 85) — 'intelligence, reason, planning-capacity, mind' — is the divine faculty the slaughtered god contributes to humankind (explicit again at I:238, *qadu ṭēmišu* 'together with his ṭēmu'). The passage turns on TWO puns, standard since Lambert–Millard and analysed by Moran (1970) and Abusch (1998): *Wê + ila → awīlu* 'man,' and *ṭēmu → eṭemmu* 'ghost.' Thus the human (*awīlu*) is named from the god (Wê-ila) and the human ghost (*eṭemmu*) from the god's intelligence (*ṭēmu*) — the being and the spirit of humankind both etymologically derived from the slain god. **Explicit lens-discipline note:** *ṭēmu* is rendered 'intelligence/reason' plainly; the lens-temptation to read it as an engineered or downloaded cognitive faculty is declined — the text says the god's reason enters humanity, and the rendering says exactly that, no more.

entries.source: i-na ši-ir i-li ù da-mi … (d)nin-tu li-ba-al-li-il ṭi-iṭ-ṭa
entries.translit: šīr ili u dami; ṭiṭṭa liballil
entries.strongs: CAD Š/3 113–121 s.v. šīru; CAD D 75–80 s.v. damu; CAD Ṭ 106–110 s.v. ṭīṭu; AHw 1248 / 158 / 1393
entries.partOfSpeech: Akkadian noun-triad — the substances of human creation (flesh, blood, clay)
entries.literal: the flesh (šīru) and blood (damu) of the god, mixed into the clay (ṭiṭṭu)
entries.standardEnglish: flesh, blood, and clay — uniform across editions (Lambert–Millard 1969; Foster 2005; Bottéro–Kramer 1989)
entries.wohChoice: render flesh / blood / clay plainly; read the three as a unified anthropogonic creation-vocabulary triad, cross-corpus to Hebrew *bāśār* / *dām* / *ʿāfār*–*ḥōmer*
entries.rationale: The individual glosses are uncontested and *ṭiṭṭu* 'clay' already has central coverage (`im-sumerian-clay-of-human-creation-cross-corpus`); what THIS entry asserts is the TRIAD as a single anthropogonic creation-vocabulary cluster. *šīru* 'flesh' (CAD Š/3 113) + *damu* 'blood' (CAD D 75) are the two DIVINE substances kneaded into the clay (I:212–215, 224–225): humankind is clay animated by a god's flesh and blood. Comparative scholarship (Kilmer 1972; Moran 1970; Batto 1992; Clifford 1994) treats the 'blood of a slain god' anthropogony as the defining Mesopotamian creation-motif, set against the Genesis 2:7 pattern where the human is *ʿāfār min hā-ʾădāmâ* 'dust from the ground' animated by *nišmat ḥayyîm* 'the breath of life' — clay/dust shared, but Genesis has NO slain deity and NO blood (a contrast, not an identity). The labor-purpose here also stands against Genesis 1:26–27, where humankind is made in the divine *ṣelem/dĕmût* to rule, not to serve — the 'labor-vs-image' contrast (Middleton 2005; Clifford 1994). **CENTRAL-GLOSSARY CANDIDATE:** this triad should be promoted to a dedicated central entry wiring Akkadian *šīru/damu/ṭiṭṭu* ↔ Hebrew *bāśār/dām/ʿāfār–ḥōmer* → Genesis 2:7, to be handled in the separate central-glossary (Python) step — deliberately NOT committed to the ~4 MB central file in this pass. claim_type `inferred` because the entry's distinctive claim is the cross-corpus cluster-identification (a named-scholarship comparative reading), not the plain glosses (which are direct facts).

entries.source: a-na du-úr da-ar up-pa i ni-iš-me
entries.translit: ana dūr dāri uppa i nišme
entries.strongs: CAD U/W 181–182 s.v. uppu; Abusch 1998 ('Ghost and God'); Lambert–Millard 1969, 153
entries.partOfSpeech: Akkadian noun — 'drum'(?); classic crux
entries.literal: the drum(?) / the throb
entries.standardEnglish: the drum (Lambert–Millard 1969)
entries.wohChoice: 'the drum(?)' — Lambert–Millard baseline, marked uncertain; the heartbeat/pulse and ghost-token readings documented
entries.rationale: *uppu* in *ana dūr dāri uppa i nišme* 'for all time let us hear the *uppu*' is a classic crux with three readings: (a) 'drum' (Lambert–Millard 1969), a cultic instrument; (b) the heartbeat/pulse — the throb that marks life; (c) a token/sign of the ghost's continued presence. Abusch (1998, 'Ghost and God') ties *uppu* to the *eṭemmu* and the *ittu* 'sign' of the following line (I:218): the throb the living 'hear' is the drum-beat of the indwelling ghost — the sign that the human carries the slain god's spirit. The Editor retains the Lambert–Millard 'drum(?)' in the text (marked uncertain, as the draft has it) and documents the heartbeat and ghost-token readings in commentary; the choice is not adjudicated and no translation change is made.

entries.strongs: CAD U/W 265 s.v. urû; AHw 1435; Lambert–Millard 1969, 62–63
entries.partOfSpeech: Akkadian noun — 'freedom'(?) / 'birth-stool'(?); crux
entries.literal: freedom / release (?) — or the birth-stool
entries.standardEnglish: freedom(?) (Lambert–Millard 1969, tentative)
entries.wohChoice: 'freedom(?)' — retained with the birth-stool alternative noted
entries.rationale: In *apṭur abšānam aškun urûtam* 'I have loosed the yoke, I have established *urûtam*,' the noun is disputed: (a) 'freedom/release,' giving the antithetical parallelism loosed-yoke // established-freedom (Lambert–Millard 1969, marked tentative); (b) 'the birth-stool,' the physical *urû* of childbirth (AHw 1435), which fits the surrounding birth-goddess context and the fourteen-pieces / birth-brick material that immediately follows. The Editor retains 'freedom(?)' as primary on the parallelism argument, marked uncertain, and notes the birth-stool reading in commentary. No adjudication; verification-pending flagged.

entries.strongs: CAD R 435–437 s.v. ruʾtu; AHw 999
entries.partOfSpeech: Akkadian noun — 'spittle, saliva'
entries.literal: with their spittle they filled / covered the clay
entries.standardEnglish: spat upon the clay (Lambert–Millard 1969; Foster 2005)
entries.wohChoice: 'spat upon the clay' — the plain, standard rendering; the interpretive question of the act's function reserved for commentary
entries.rationale: *ruʾtu* 'spittle' (CAD R 435) is uncontested; the Igigi 'spat upon the clay' (I:233). What is interpretively open is the act's FUNCTION: (a) animation of the clay; (b) ritual ratification / collective assent to the creation (the Igigi endorse it corporately); (c) contribution of a further divine bodily-substance — so that ALL the Igigi, not only the one slain god, add themselves to humankind (alongside the flesh and blood). The Editor keeps the plain rendering and reserves the interpretive options for commentary; no reading is imported into the text. **Explicit lens-discipline note:** the 'spittle as animating agent' reading is declined in the surface text — the line says the gods spat on the clay, and the rendering says exactly that.

entries.strongs: CAD R 328–334 s.v. rigmu; CAD Ḫ 218–220 s.v. ḫubūru B ('noise, din'); AHw 982 / 352
entries.partOfSpeech: Akkadian nouns — 'noise / cry / clamor' and 'din / uproar' of a too-numerous humankind; the narrative engine of Tablet II and the stated flood-cause
entries.literal: the noise (rigmu) of humankind; at their clamor / din (ḫubūru)
entries.standardEnglish: noise / clamor / uproar / din — uniform across editions (Lambert–Millard 1969; Foster 2005; Bottéro–Kramer 1989)
entries.wohChoice: render *rigmu* 'noise' and *ḫubūru* 'clamor / uproar' plainly; the overpopulation framing is left implicit in the line (it is already explicit in Enlil's grievance) and is NOT editorialized into the text
entries.rationale: *rigmu* (CAD R 328) 'voice, cry, noise' and *ḫubūru* (CAD Ḫ 218, ḫubūru B) 'noise, din, uproar' are the recurring terms for the sound of a swelling humankind that robs Enlil of sleep (II i 3–4, 6–7; ii 18; iii 3–4, 6; vi 4) and that the Flood is sent to silence (III iii 7, where Anzû/the deluge 'stills its clamor'). The plain glosses are direct and uncontested; what THIS entry asserts — and why the claim_type is `inferred` rather than `direct` — is the reading, foundational since Kilmer (1972) and Moran (1971), that the *rigmu/ḫubūru* is the noise of OVERPOPULATION, so that the successive afflictions and finally the Flood function as divine POPULATION-CONTROL. This same *rigmu*-as-flood-cause appears in Gilgamesh XI (the gods resolve on the flood because of humankind's clamor) and stands in pointed CONTRAST to the Genesis flood, whose cause is moral: *ḥāmās* 'violence' filling the earth (Gen 6:11–13) and, at Sodom, the *ṣeʿāqâ* 'outcry' of injustice (Gen 18:20–21) — noise-vs-corruption, a contrast, not an identity. Note a homonym to be kept separate: at III iii 15 (*rigim abūbi*) and III ii 28 *rigmu* denotes the ROAR of the storm/Adad, not the human clamor; those occurrences are excluded from this entry's scope. **CENTRAL-GLOSSARY CANDIDATE:** propose promoting *rigmu/ḫubūru* to a dedicated central entry wiring the Akkadian clamor ↔ the Gilgamesh XI flood-cause ↔ Hebrew *ḥāmās*/*ṣeʿāqâ*, to be handled in the separate central-glossary (Python) step — deliberately NOT committed to the ~4 MB central file here. **Lens-discipline note:** the overpopulation reading is mainstream Assyriology and is allowed to stand in the apparatus, but it is kept OUT of the translated line (which says only 'noise' / 'clamor'); the interpretive Elohim-frame identification of a population-managing civilization is escalated to the Explainer, not the text.

entries.strongs: CAD N/1 247 s.v. namtaru ('fate; the god of death/plague'); AHw 729; Lambert–Millard 1969, 66–73
entries.partOfSpeech: Akkadian/Sumerian divine name — the plague/fate-god Enlil dispatches to reduce humankind
entries.literal: Namtar (Sumerian NAM.TAR 'fate, that which is decreed')
entries.standardEnglish: Namtar (retained; Lambert–Millard 1969; Foster 2005)
entries.wohChoice: retain 'Namtar' untranslated as a divine name; apply only the DINGIR-prefix-prose-drop convention
entries.rationale: *Namtar* (CAD N/1 247, from Sumerian NAM.TAR 'fate') is both the abstract 'fate/decree' and the netherworld deity of death and pestilence who serves as vizier of Ereškigal; in Tablet II he is the agent of Enlil's first affliction, dispatched to 'diminish the noise' of humankind by plague (II i 9–10) and later the god at whose 'door' the people concentrate their offering (II ii 14, 18). The Editor retains the name untranslated, consistent with the project's treatment of the other divine names in the poem (Adad, Nisaba, Ea, Enlil), rather than rendering the function ('Fate', 'the plague-god'), because the name is a fixed proper noun in the tradition and the plague-function is already clear from the narrative. The wordplay latent in the name (NAM.TAR 'the decreed thing' → the decreed pestilence) is noted in commentary, not imported into the line; no lens is carried.

entries.source: (d)adad zu-un-na-šu li-šá-aq-qir; li-še-eṣ-ṣi i-na mu-ši-im na-al-šu
entries.translit: Adad zunnašu lišaqqir; lišēṣṣi ina mūšim nalšu
entries.strongs: CAD A/1 51–52 s.v. Adad; CAD Z 156 s.v. zunnu ('rain'); AHw 1537; central entry adad-hadad-baal-storm-god-flood-instrument-cross-corpus
entries.partOfSpeech: convention / scope-note — the INVERTED (drought) role of the storm-god Adad in Tablet II, against his flood-instrument role elsewhere
entries.literal: let Adad make his rain precious (i.e. scarce / withhold it); let him send down his dew stealthily in the night
entries.standardEnglish: let Adad withhold his rain / hold back the rain (Lambert–Millard 1969; Foster 2005)
entries.wohChoice: render the drought-function plainly ('let Adad withhold his rain'; 'send down his dew … rain down stealthily like dew'); apply the central Adad entry by id for the NAME identity, and flag the drought-role for Akkadian-side appliesTo activation + a scope note in the central step
entries.rationale: The central entry `adad-hadad-baal-storm-god-flood-instrument-cross-corpus` frames Adad as the storm-god who is the INSTRUMENT of the Flood (his role in Tablet III ii 27–33 and Gilgamesh XI). In Tablet II his role is the INVERSE: Enlil orders him to WITHHOLD the rain (*zunnašu lišaqqir*, lit. 'make his rain precious/scarce', II iii 7) so drought and famine thin humankind — the black fields whiten and the plain brings forth salt — and then, under Enki's stratagem, Adad RELENTS, sending down a stealthy night-dew (*ina mūšim nalšu*, II iv 13–14). The name-identity is covered centrally (id in glossaryRefs); this overlay entry records the drought-scope so the reader sees that the SAME storm-god is the withholder-of-rain here and the sender-of-flood there — the storm powers both the drought (rain denied) and the deluge (rain unleashed). The Editor renders each function plainly and flags the Tablet-II drought lines for Akkadian-side `appliesTo` activation on the central entry, with a scope note (storm-as-flood vs storm-withheld-as-drought), deferred to the central (Python) step; no new central sub-node is created here.

entries.source: e ta-ap-la-ḫa i-li-ku-un … bi-il-la a-na pa-ni-šu ma-aṣ-ḫa-tam … li-ba-aš i-na kad-ri-šu-ma li-is-suḫ qá-as-su; wa-ar-ki-šu (d)é-a te-ma iš-ku-un
entries.translit: ē taplaḫā ilīkun … billā ana pānišu maṣḫatam … libâš ina kadrišu-ma lissuḫ qāssu; warkišu Ea ṭēma iškun
entries.strongs: CAD B 5–8 s.v. bâšu ('to be ashamed'); CAD K 33 s.v. kadru/kadrû ('gift, offering'); CAD N/2 3–14 s.v. nasāḫu ('to remove'); CAD Ṭ 85–98 s.v. ṭēmu ('plan, counsel, instruction')
entries.partOfSpeech: Akkadian idiom-cluster — Enki's repeated stratagem: concentrate all offerings on one god so that, shamed, he lifts the scourge; with the Tablet-II sense of ṭēmu ('plan/scheme')
entries.literal: do not reverence your gods … carry a flour-offering before him … let him be shamed by the gift and pull away his hand; Ea had set the plan (ṭēmu) behind it
entries.standardEnglish: withhold reverence, bring the offering to the one god, let him be shamed and lift the affliction (Lambert–Millard 1969; Foster 2005)
entries.wohChoice: render the stratagem plainly across its two occurrences; render Tablet-II *ṭēmu* as 'plan' / 'scheme'; do NOT apply the Tablet-I anthropogonic ṭēmu-pun entry here
entries.rationale: Twice in Tablet II (the plague, ii 11–17; the drought, iv 7–14) Enki instructs Atra-ḫasīs on the same stratagem: have the people WITHHOLD reverence from all the gods (*ē taplaḫā*, negative precative) and concentrate every offering (*maṣḫatu* flour-offering, *niqû* offering) on the SINGLE deity responsible for the current scourge (Namtar; then Adad), so that god — *bâšu* 'shamed' (CAD B 5) by the *kadrû* 'gift' (CAD K 33) arriving at his door alone — lifts the affliction (*nasāḫu qāta*, lit. 'pull away the hand'). This offering-concentration/shaming-the-god device is the interpretive spine of Tablet II and turns on the Mesopotamian economy in which gods DEPEND on human offerings (the same dependency that later leaves them starving during the Flood, III iv 16–19). **Critical distinction, per the editorial question:** the *ṭēmu* at II vii 1 (*Ea ṭēma iškun* 'Ea had set the ṭēmu/plan behind it') carries the sense 'plan, scheme, counsel, instruction' (CAD Ṭ 85, senses 3–5) — the clever design by which Ea repeatedly thwarts Enlil — and is therefore rendered 'plan'/'scheme'. This is a DIFFERENT sense from the Tablet-I anthropogonic *ṭēmu* (the slain god's 'intelligence/reason' that becomes the human *eṭemmu*, I 222/238); the overlay entry `we-ila-temu-anthropogonic-pun-atrahasis` is deliberately NOT applied to Tablet II, and the two senses are kept unconflated. No lens is carried: the stratagem and the plan are rendered exactly as the Akkadian states them.

entries.strongs: CAD Š/3 411 s.v. šuruppû ('frost, chills-disease'); CAD D 165 s.v. diʾu (a febrile disease); CAD B 301 s.v. bubūtu ('hunger, famine'); CAD I/J 10 s.v. idrānu ('saltpetre, natron, salt')
entries.partOfSpeech: Akkadian nouns — the successive afflictions sent to reduce humankind: chills-disease, fever-sickness, famine, and the drought's salt
entries.literal: the chills-disease (šuruppû); the fever-sickness (diʾu); hunger / famine (bubūtu); saltpetre / salt (idrānu)
entries.standardEnglish: the chills / frost-disease, sickness, famine, salt (Lambert–Millard 1969; Foster 2005)
entries.wohChoice: render each affliction plainly — *šuruppû* 'the chills-disease', *diʾu* 'sickness', *bubūtu* 'famine', *idrānu* 'salt' (the drought's 'black fields turned white') — with no interpretive expansion
entries.rationale: Tablet II deploys a distinct affliction-vocabulary that the glossary did not previously cover: *šuruppû* (CAD Š/3 411) the 'chills/frost' pestilence Enlil first unleashes (II i 8; ii 8, where 'your šuruppû is devouring the land'); *diʾu* (CAD D 165) the febrile 'sickness' set within the people (II i 10); *bubūtu* (CAD B 301) 'hunger/famine', the third scourge (II iv 4; recurring for the gods' own hunger at III iv 16–19 and as a post-flood check at III vi 24); and *idrānu* (CAD I/J 10) 'saltpetre/salt', the sign of the drought's ruin as 'the black fields turn white' and 'the broad plain brings forth salt' (II iii 11–12). Each is rendered plainly; the glosses are uncontested. The afflictions form a coherent sequence — pestilence, then drought/famine — that the mainstream reading (Kilmer 1972) treats as instruments of divine POPULATION-CONTROL, escalating toward the Flood; that reading is allowed in the apparatus but the lexemes stay plain in the line. **Flagged (not committed) as a possible central 'divine population-control afflictions' cluster** for the separate central step; not asserted as a cross-corpus claim here.

entries.strongs: CAD A/2 495 s.v. atru ('surpassing, excess'); CAD Ḫ 126 s.v. ḫasīsu ('wisdom, understanding, ear'); central entry ziusudra-atrahasis-utnapishtim-noach-flood-survivor-name-cluster-cross-corpus
entries.partOfSpeech: Akkadian proper name — the flood-hero; etymologically 'exceedingly wise'
entries.literal: Atra-ḫasīs = *atra* 'surpassing / exceeding(ly)' + *ḫasīsu* 'wisdom, understanding' → 'exceedingly wise'
entries.standardEnglish: Atra-ḫasīs (retained; 'Atrahasis'); the name means 'exceedingly wise' (Lambert–Millard 1969; Foster 2005)
entries.wohChoice: retain 'Atra-ḫasīs' untranslated (per the central survivor-name cluster); gloss the etymology 'the exceedingly-wise' in commentary on first occurrence in each tablet; flag the central cluster's Akkadian-side appliesTo activation
entries.rationale: The protagonist's name, *Atra(m)-ḫasīs*, is transparently 'exceedingly wise': *atra* 'surpassing, in excess' (CAD A/2 495) + *ḫasīsu* 'wisdom, understanding, (the discerning) ear' (CAD Ḫ 126) — the very epithet that marks him as the sage who 'keeps his ear open' to Ea (II ii 2) and is chosen to survive. The Editor retains the name untranslated, following the central survivor-name cluster `ziusudra-atrahasis-utnapishtim-noach-flood-survivor-name-cluster-cross-corpus` (which files him with Sumerian Ziusudra 'life of long days', Akkadian Ūta-napišti 'he found life', and Hebrew Noaḥ), and glosses the meaning in commentary on the name's first occurrence in Tablet II (ii 1) and Tablet III (ii 10) rather than inserting a parenthetical into the line. The name is the composition's title. The central cluster's `appliesTo` currently lists Sumerian-Flood-Story refIds only; the Akkadian occurrences are flagged for `appliesTo` activation in the separate central step. No lens is carried; the etymology is a plain philological fact.

entries.source: i-ga-ru ši-ta-am-mi-a-an-ni; ki-ik-ki-šu ṣú-ur-ri ka-la zi-ik-ri-ia
entries.translit: igāru šitammiânni; kikkišu ṣurri kala zikriya
entries.strongs: CAD I/J 33–39 s.v. igāru ('wall'); CAD K 352 s.v. kikkišu ('reed fence, reed hut wall'); central entries iz-zi-da-kikkish-talking-through-the-wall-to-keep-an-oath-flood-trope-cross-corpus; ea-warning-deception-misadvice-test-crux-cross-corpus
entries.partOfSpeech: Akkadian nouns — the (reed) wall Enki addresses to warn Atra-ḫasīs without breaking his oath
entries.literal: 'Wall, listen closely to me! Reed wall, attend to all my words!'
entries.standardEnglish: 'Reed wall … ' / 'Wall, hear me! Reed-fence, heed my words!' (Lambert–Millard 1969; parallel to Gilgamesh XI 21–22)
entries.wohChoice: render the doubled apostrophe plainly — 'Wall, listen closely to me! reed wall, attend to all my words!'; apply the central reed-wall and Ea-warning trope entries by id, flagging Akkadian-side appliesTo activation
entries.rationale: *igāru* 'wall' (CAD I/J 33) paired with *kikkišu* 'reed fence / reed-hut wall' (CAD K 352) is the device by which Enki keeps the letter of the divine oath (*māmītu*) not to warn a human of the Flood directly: he speaks INTO the reed wall of Atra-ḫasīs's hut, so the man 'overhears' and Enki can later plead (III vi 13–14) that he 'did not reveal the command of the gods'. This talking-through-the-wall oath-loophole is a cross-corpus flood-trope (Sumerian Flood Story; famously Gilgamesh XI 21–22, *kikkiš kikkiš igār igār* 'Reed-fence, reed-fence! Wall, wall!'), covered by the central entries `iz-zi-da-kikkish-talking-through-the-wall-to-keep-an-oath-flood-trope-cross-corpus` and `ea-warning-deception-misadvice-test-crux-cross-corpus`; this overlay entry anchors the specific Akkadian Atra-ḫasīs wording and flags those central entries for Akkadian-side `appliesTo` activation. The Editor keeps the plainer doubling attested in the Atra-ḫasīs lines rather than importing the fuller Gilgamesh reduplication. The oath-loophole is rendered as narrated; the interpretive 'was Enki deceiving or testing?' question belongs to the central Ea-warning crux, not the line.

entries.source: na-pí-iš-ta bu-ul-li-iṭ; e-eš-ta uṣ-ṣí-a-am na-pí-iš-tum; aš-šum na-ap-ša-tim uš-te-ṣi
entries.translit: napišta bulliṭ; ēšta uṣṣiam napištum; aššum napšātim uštēṣi
entries.strongs: CAD N/1 296–304 s.v. napištu ('life, throat, living being'); CAD B 60–63 s.v. balāṭu, D-stem bulluṭu ('to keep alive, preserve'); AHw 738 / 99
entries.partOfSpeech: Akkadian noun + verb — the instruction to 'keep life alive' / preserve the living
entries.literal: keep life (napištu) alive (bulliṭ, D-imperative); 'where did life escape?'; 'because of life I brought (it) out'
entries.standardEnglish: keep life / living things alive; save life (Lambert–Millard 1969; Foster 2005)
entries.wohChoice: 'Spurn possessions and keep life alive!' — render *napišta bulliṭ* as 'keep life alive' / 'save life'; *napištu* as 'life, living things', not the reflexive 'save your own life'
entries.rationale: *napištu* (CAD N/1 296) is 'life, throat, breath, living being', and the D-stem of *balāṭu* (*bulluṭu*, CAD B 60) is factitive 'to keep alive, preserve, save'; Enki's charge *makkūra zērma napišta bulliṭ* (III i 14) is therefore 'spurn possessions and keep LIFE alive' — the seed of humankind and the living creatures Atra-ḫasīs loads onto the boat, not merely his own survival. The same root frames the flood's aftermath: Enlil's furious 'where did *napištu* escape?' / 'how did a man survive?' (III vi 9–10) and Enki's confession 'because of *napšātu* (life) I brought (it) out' (III vi 18). The Editor renders 'keep life alive' / 'save life', collective, rejecting the reflexive 'save your own life' because the narrative point (and the preservation-of-the-seed flood-aitia carried centrally by `preservation-of-the-seed-of-humankind-and-animals-flood-aitia-cross-corpus`) is the rescue of life as such. Comparative note for commentary: the same instruction underlies Genesis 6:19–20 ('to keep them alive with you', *lĕhaḥăyôt*) and 7:3 ('to keep seed alive', *lĕḥayyôt zeraʿ*). No lens is carried.

entries.source: li-ib-ši i-na ni-ši pa-ši-it-tu; li-iṣ-ba-at še-er-ra i-na bi-ir-ki a-li-it-ti
entries.translit: libši ina nišī pašittu; liṣbat šerra ina birki ālitti
entries.strongs: CAD P 253 s.v. pašittu (a demon); AHw 845; Lambert–Millard 1969, 102–103, 163
entries.partOfSpeech: Akkadian noun — a female demon who snatches the newborn; one of the permanent post-flood checks on human fertility
entries.literal: the pašittu (from *pašāṭu* 'to erase/blot out'?), 'let her seize the baby from the lap of her who bore it'
entries.standardEnglish: the pašittu-demon / the 'Eradicator' (Lambert–Millard 1969); a stillbirth/infant-mortality demoness (Foster 2005)
entries.wohChoice: retain *pašittu* transliterated, glossed 'the pašittu-demon' — as Tablet I retained *lullû* and *eṭemmu*
entries.rationale: *pašittu* (CAD P 253; probably from *pašāṭu* 'to blot out, erase') is a female demon of the birth-chamber, established in the poem's etiological close as a permanent check on human numbers: 'let there be among the peoples the *pašittu*, to snatch the baby from the lap of her who bore it' (III vii 8–9) — the mythic aetiology of infant mortality and stillbirth. The Editor retains the term transliterated with a descriptive gloss, following the Tablet-I precedent for technical anthropogonic/demonic keywords (*lullû*, *eṭemmu*), rather than flattening it to 'the snatcher' or over-specifying to 'the stillbirth-demon', neither of which is consensus. The *pašittu* belongs to the DELIBERATE population-limiting apparatus that closes Atra-ḫasīs: the gods, having decided not to repeat the total Flood, install standing limits on fertility so the human *rigmu* never again grows unbearable — a reading that is explicit in the Akkadian (Kilmer 1972; Lambert–Millard 1969) and is rendered plainly. No lens is carried.

entries.strongs: CAD A/1 341 s.v. ālittu ('woman who has given birth, mother'); CAD (lā + participle, negation); AHw 38
entries.partOfSpeech: Akkadian noun-pair — 'the woman who bears' and 'the woman who does not bear'; the institution of childlessness as a population check
entries.literal: the bearing woman (ālittu) and the not-bearing woman (lā ālittu)
entries.standardEnglish: the woman who bears and the woman who does not bear (Lambert–Millard 1969; Foster 2005)
entries.wohChoice: render 'the woman who bears and the woman who does not bear' — plain; no transliteration needed
entries.rationale: *ālittu* (CAD A/1 341, from *alādu* 'to give birth') is 'a woman who has borne, a mother'; the poem's close establishes alongside her the *lā ālittu*, 'the woman who does NOT bear' (III vii 7), as a permanent human category — barrenness/childlessness instituted, like the *pašittu*-demon and the celibate priestesses, to cap human fertility after the Flood. The phrase is rendered plainly and needs no transliteration (unlike the demon- and priestess-names it is ordinary descriptive vocabulary). This entry documents its place in the etiological population-limit cluster: the three devices — non-bearing women, the infant-snatching *pašittu*, and the celibate priestess classes — together with settled mortality are the gods' DELIBERATE, standing replacement for the one-off Flood, the mechanism by which the human clamor (`rigmu-huburu-...`) is permanently held in check. This is stated in the Akkadian and is rendered without lens.

entries.source: šu-uk-ni ug-ba-ak-ka-ti en-e-ti ù i-gi-ṣi-a-ti; lu ik-ki-bu-ma a-la-da pu-ur-si
entries.translit: šukni ugbakkāti enēti u igiṣiāti; lu ikkibū-ma alāda pursi
entries.strongs: CAD U/W 25 s.v. ugbabtu; CAD E 172 s.v. ēntu; CAD I/J 44 s.v. igiṣītu; CAD I/J 55 s.v. ikkibu ('taboo, forbidden thing')
entries.partOfSpeech: Akkadian nouns — three classes of cultic priestess placed under a birth-taboo as a permanent fertility check
entries.literal: establish the ugbabtu, entu, and igiṣītu (priestess classes); let them be under taboo (ikkibu), and so cut off childbirth
entries.standardEnglish: the ugbabtu / entu / igiṣītu priestesses, for whom childbearing is taboo (Lambert–Millard 1969; Foster 2005)
entries.wohChoice: retain *ugbabtu*, *entu*, *igiṣītu* transliterated with the gloss 'priestesses' and render *ikkibu* 'taboo' — 'let them be under taboo, and so cut off childbirth'
entries.rationale: The poem closes its population-limit apparatus with three cultic offices whose members are forbidden to bear: the *ugbabtu* (CAD U/W 25, a high-ranking priestess/votary), the *ēntu* (CAD E 172, the high priestess, often royal), and the *igiṣītu* (CAD I/J 44, a class of votary), for whom childbirth is made an *ikkibu* — 'taboo, an abomination, a forbidden thing' (CAD I/J 55): *lu ikkibū-ma alāda pursi* 'let them be under taboo, and so cut off childbirth' (III vii 10–11). The Editor retains the three office-names transliterated (they are technical cultic titles with no exact English equivalent, following the Tablet-I precedent for *lullû*/*eṭemmu*) and renders *ikkibu* 'taboo'. Historically these lines are the mythic charter for real Old Babylonian institutions of celibate/childless priestesses (the *nadītu* and related classes), here retrojected as a divinely-instituted brake on population — the deliberate fertility-cap that, with the *pašittu*, the *lā ālittu*, and settled mortality, replaces the Flood. The reading is explicit in the Akkadian (Kilmer 1972) and is rendered plainly, without lens.

entries.strongs: CAD M/2 317–318 s.v. mūtu ('death'); AHw 691; central entry return-to-the-earth-mortality-verdict-adapa-genesis-cross-corpus
entries.partOfSpeech: Akkadian noun — 'death'; here the establishment of settled human mortality as the etiological verdict of the flood-aftermath
entries.literal: establish death (mūtu) for the peoples
entries.standardEnglish: establish death for the people / appoint death for mankind (Lambert–Millard 1969; Foster 2005)
entries.wohChoice: 'establish death for the peoples' — *mūtu* as the permanent human CONDITION (mortality), not a 'death-demon'; apply the central mortality-verdict entry by id, flagging Akkadian-side activation
entries.rationale: *mūtu* (CAD M/2 317) is 'death'; Enki's charge to Nintu *šukni mūta ana nišī* 'establish death for the peoples' (III vii 4) is the etiological climax of the whole composition — humankind, created in Tablet I to be effectively perpetual labor, is now made permanently MORTAL so that its numbers, and its clamor, are self-limiting. The Editor reads *mūtu* here as the CONDITION/verdict of mortality (parallel to the mortality-verdicts of Adapa and Genesis 3, and covered cross-corpus by the central entry `return-to-the-earth-mortality-verdict-adapa-genesis-cross-corpus`), not as a personified 'death-demon' on the model of the *pašittu* of the following lines; the plural etiological frame ('for the peoples', not 'upon a mother') and the pairing with the fertility-checks support the condition-reading. The Akkadian-side occurrence is flagged for `appliesTo` activation on the central entry in the separate step. Comparative note for commentary: this is the Mesopotamian settling of the death-question that the biblical primeval history places in Eden (Gen 3:19, 'to dust you shall return'). The line is rendered plainly; no lens is carried, and the interpretive Elohim-frame reading of an engineered lifespan-limit is escalated to the Explainer, not the text.
